title: Lifestyle and Sleep Quality in College Students
text:
This STAT 330 project examines which academic, behavioral, psychological, and circadian characteristics are associated with poor sleep quality among undergraduate students. Using the SleepStudy dataset, the analysis focuses on predicting sleep disruption—not establishing that any one characteristic causes it.
The response, poor sleep quality, is measured on a scale from 1 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater disruption. The dataset includes 253 student observations and measures such as anxiety status, depression, happiness, classes missed, weekday sleep, bedtime, and chronotype.

Key findings: Anxiety status and classes missed were the clearest individual predictors in the selected model. Students reporting normal anxiety were predicted to have sleep-disruption scores 1.32 points lower, on average, than students in the moderate-anxiety reference group. Each additional missed class was associated with a 0.10-point increase in the predicted score, holding the other model terms constant.

Students reporting normal anxiety were predicted to have sleep-disruption scores 1.32 points lower, on average, than students in the moderate-anxiety reference group. Each additional missed class was associated with a 0.10-point increase in the predicted score, holding the other model terms constant.
crumbs: Lifestyle and Sleep Quality in College Students

title: Lifestyle and Sleep Quality in College Students
text:
Modeling approach
The team first explored multiple linear regression for cognitive performance, but its explanatory power was low. The project then focused on poor sleep quality, for which candidate models explained more variation. LASSO regularization screened potential predictors; best-subset models were compared using adjusted R², Mallows’ Cₚ, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and 10-fold cross-validation.
The selected model balanced interpretability and predictive performance, including main effects and interactions among sleep, mood, anxiety, and chronotype measures. Its cross-validated root mean squared error (RMSE) was approximately 2.39 points on the 1–18 response scale. The report describes the model as explaining about 35% of the variation in sleep-disruption scores.
crumbs: Lifestyle and Sleep Quality in College Students

title: Lifestyle and Sleep Quality in College Students
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The results suggest that psychological health and class attendance may be useful markers when describing sleep quality in this student sample. The selected model also retained some terms that were not individually statistically significant; their inclusion supported the model’s overall predictive performance. The report’s diagnostics found the linear-regression assumptions reasonably satisfied.
These are associations from an observational dataset, so they should not be interpreted as evidence that anxiety, attendance, or other measured characteristics directly cause changes in sleep. The findings are also limited to the students and measures represented in the dataset.

title: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis
text:
This project examines how food prices in the United States have changed over the past decade using the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It explores three questions: how food-price trends vary across categories, whether prices show seasonal patterns, and how recent inflation compares with the Federal Reserve’s general 2% inflation target.
The CPI tracks changes over time in the prices consumers pay for a representative basket of goods and services. This analysis focuses on food, connecting national price trends to a familiar part of household budgets.
crumbs: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis

title: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis
text:
This project examines how food prices in the United States have changed over the past decade using the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It explores three questions: how food-price trends vary across categories, whether prices show seasonal patterns, and how recent inflation compares with the Federal Reserve’s general 2% inflation target.
The CPI tracks changes over time in the prices consumers pay for a representative basket of goods and services. This analysis focuses on food, connecting national price trends to a familiar part of household budgets.
crumbs: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis

title: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis
text:
Data and methods
The analysis combines monthly CPI data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics with annual food-category CPI data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The datasets were cleaned and reshaped in R using the tidyverse to support comparisons over time and across food groups.
Month-over-month and year-over-year percentage changes were calculated to describe short-term movement and longer-term inflation. Visualizations made with ggplot2 were used to investigate seasonal patterns, compare food categories, and show how food-price inflation changed relative to the 2% benchmark.
crumbs: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis

title: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis
text:
Key findings

Food prices showed mild seasonal variation, tending to be higher earlier in the year.
Overall inflation was near 2% before 2020, rose above 6% after 2020, and later moderated to around 3%.
Inflation patterns varied by food category. Eggs were the most volatile of the categories examined, while many categories peaked around 2022 and declined afterward.
crumbs: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis

title: Consumer Price Index: Food Cost Analysis
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The results show that food-price changes vary over time and across categories; the overall inflation benchmark does not describe every food group equally. The CPI is an index of average price change, so it does not represent the exact grocery costs or buying patterns of every household. The analysis is descriptive: it identifies trends and seasonal patterns but does not explain their causes.

title: Learning About the Python Library: RapidFuzz
text:
Overview
In this tutorial, we will explore the Python library RapidFuzz, which is a powerful tool for string matching and fuzzy searching. RapidFuzz is designed to be fast and efficient, making it an excellent choice for tasks that involve comparing strings or finding similar matches.
I first came across RapidFuzz while working on a project to categorize financial data from bank statements. I needed a way to quickly and accurately match transaction descriptions to predefined categories, and RapidFuzz provided the perfect solution.
We will focus on the following key features of RapidFuzz:

String matching and similarity scoring
Fuzzy searching and partial matching
Performance optimization techniques

As we go through this tutorial, I will share some examples of how to use RapidFuzz effectively. I encourage you to try out these concepts in our own projects. By the end of this tutorial, you should have a solid understanding of how to use RapidFuzz effectively in Python applications. Let’s get started!

title: Learning About the Python Library: RapidFuzz
text:
Installation
To install RapidFuzz, you can use pip, the Python package manager. Open your terminal and run the following command:
pip install rapidfuzz
This will download and install the RapidFuzz library, allowing you to use it in your Python projects.
An alternative method is to install it via uv if you are using a virtual environment:
uv add rapidfuzz
Once you have RapidFuzz installed, you can import it in your Python code as shown below and start using its features for string matching and fuzzy searching.
from rapidfuzz import fuzz, process
In the next sections, we will dive deeper into the functionalities of RapidFuzz and see how it can be applied to various string matching tasks.

title: Learning About the Python Library: RapidFuzz
text:
String Matching and Similarity Scoring
RapidFuzz provides several functions for string matching and similarity scoring. The most commonly used function is fuzz.ratio(), which calculates the similarity ratio between two strings. The ratio is a value between 0 and 100, where 100 means the strings are identical. Here’s an example of how to use fuzz.ratio():


Code
from rapidfuzz import fuzz
string1 = "Hello, World!"
string2 = "Hello, World!"
similarity = fuzz.ratio(string1, string2)
print(f"Similarity Ratio: {similarity}%")


Similarity Ratio: 100.0%


In this example, since both strings are identical, the similarity ratio will be 100%. You can also compare different strings to see how closely they match:


Code
string1 = "Hello, World!"
string2 = "Hello, World"
similarity = fuzz.ratio(string1, string2)
print(f"Similarity Ratio: {similarity}%")


Similarity Ratio: 96.0%


In this case, the similarity ratio will be slightly less than 100% due to the missing exclamation mark in the second string. RapidFuzz also offers other functions like fuzz.partial_ratio() and fuzz.token_sort_ratio() for more specific types of string comparisons, which we will explore in the next sections.

title: Learning About the Python Library: RapidFuzz
text:
Fuzzy Searching and Partial Matching
In addition to exact string matching, RapidFuzz excels at fuzzy searching and partial matching. The fuzz.partial_ratio() function is particularly useful for comparing substrings or when the strings being compared have different lengths. It calculates the similarity ratio based on the best matching substring. Here’s an example of how to use fuzz.partial_ratio():


Code
from rapidfuzz import fuzz
string1 = "Hello, World!"
string2 = "Hello"
similarity = fuzz.partial_ratio(string1, string2)
print(f"Partial Similarity Ratio: {similarity}%")


Partial Similarity Ratio: 100.0%


In this example, the fuzz.partial_ratio() function will return a high similarity ratio because “Hello” is a substring of “Hello, World!”. This is particularly useful when you want to find matches in larger texts or when the strings being compared may have additional characters.


Code
string1 = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog."
string2 = "quick brown fox"
similarity = fuzz.partial_ratio(string1, string2)
print(f"Partial Similarity Ratio: {similarity}%")


Partial Similarity Ratio: 100.0%


In this case, the fuzz.partial_ratio() function will return a high similarity ratio because “quick brown fox” is a substring of the larger string. RapidFuzz also provides other functions like fuzz.token_sort_ratio() and fuzz.token_set_ratio() for more complex string comparisons, which we will cover in the next section.

title: Learning About the Python Library: RapidFuzz
text:
Performance Optimization Techniques
One of the key advantages of RapidFuzz is its performance. However, when working with large datasets or performing multiple string comparisons, it’s important to optimize your code for efficiency. Here are some techniques to improve performance when using RapidFuzz:

Use the process module for batch processing: Instead of comparing strings one by one, you can use the process.extract() function to compare a query string against a list of choices. This is much faster than looping through each choice individually.



Code
from rapidfuzz import process
choices = ["Hello, World!", "Hello", "Hi there!", "Greetings"]
query = "Hello"
results = process.extract(query, choices, scorer=fuzz.ratio)
print(results)


[('Hello', 100.0, 1), ('Hello, World!', 55.55555555555556, 0), ('Hi there!', 28.57142857142857, 2), ('Greetings', 14.28571428571429, 3)]


In this example, process.extract() will return a list of choices along with their similarity scores, allowing you to quickly identify the best matches.

Limit the number of comparisons: If you have a large dataset, consider limiting the number of comparisons by filtering your choices based on certain criteria before applying RapidFuzz. This can significantly reduce the number of comparisons and improve performance.



Code
filtered_choices = [choice for choice in choices if len(choice) > 5]
results = process.extract(query, filtered_choices, scorer=fuzz.ratio)
print(results)


[('Hello, World!', 55.55555555555556, 0), ('Hi there!', 28.57142857142857, 1), ('Greetings', 14.28571428571429, 2)]


In this example, we filter the choices to only include those that are longer than 5 characters before applying the process.extract() function. This can help improve performance by reducing the number of comparisons.

Use the processor parameter: RapidFuzz allows you to specify a custom processor function to preprocess the strings before comparison. This can help improve performance by normalizing the strings (e.g., converting to lowercase, removing punctuation) and reducing the number of unique comparisons.



Code
def custom_processor(s):
    return s.lower().replace(",", "").replace("!", "")
results = process.extract(query, choices, scorer=fuzz.ratio, processor=custom_processor)
print(results)


[('Hello', 100.0, 1), ('Hello, World!', 62.5, 0), ('Hi there!', 30.76923076923077, 2), ('Greetings', 14.28571428571429, 3)]


In this example, we define a custom processor function that converts the strings to lowercase and removes punctuation before comparison. This can help improve performance by reducing the number of unique comparisons and increasing the likelihood of matches.
By implementing these performance optimization techniques, you can ensure that your use of RapidFuzz remains efficient even when working with large datasets or performing multiple string comparisons. Remember to always test and profile your code to identify any bottlenecks and optimize accordingly.

title: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment
text:
This experiment examined whether oil type and the timing of adding popcorn kernels affect total popping time. The study compared olive, vegetable, and coconut oil under two starting procedures. It was designed to distinguish the effects of each factor and determine whether the effect of kernel timing varied by oil type.

Key finding: The report concluded that the heated-start procedure took longer than the cold-start procedure (p = 0.00441). Oil type and the interaction between oil type and kernel timing were not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
crumbs: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment

title: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment
text:
This experiment examined whether oil type and the timing of adding popcorn kernels affect total popping time. The study compared olive, vegetable, and coconut oil under two starting procedures. It was designed to distinguish the effects of each factor and determine whether the effect of kernel timing varied by oil type.

Key finding: The report concluded that the heated-start procedure took longer than the cold-start procedure (p = 0.00441). Oil type and the interaction between oil type and kernel timing were not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
crumbs: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment

title: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment
text:
Study design
The team used a balanced, randomized 2 × 3 factorial design:



Factor
Conditions




Oil type
Olive, vegetable, and coconut


Kernel timing
Cold start and heated start



Each of the six treatment combinations was repeated five times, for 30 trials in total. The response variable was the time to complete popping, measured in seconds. Treatment order was randomized before data collection to reduce potential bias from trial order.
For a cold-start trial, the kernels were added to the oil at the beginning of heating. For a heated-start trial, four kernels were added first; the remaining kernels were added after the first of those kernels popped. Trials followed a consistent stovetop procedure, including a standard oil amount, medium-high heat, and a defined stopping point based on the interval between pops.
crumbs: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment

title: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment
text:
Analysis and results
A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to evaluate the effects of oil type, kernel timing, and their interaction on total popping time. At a significance level of α = 0.05, the results were:



Effect
p-value
Interpretation




Kernel timing
0.00441
Statistically significant


Oil type
0.06552
Not statistically significant


Oil type × kernel timing
0.09184
Not statistically significant



The report concluded that the heated-start procedure took longer than the cold-start procedure. The study did not find sufficient evidence that popping time differed by oil type, or that the effect of kernel timing depended on the oil used. These non-significant findings do not establish that the effects are exactly zero.
The team reviewed residual diagnostic plots and reported that the residuals were approximately normal, the randomized order supported independence, and the spread across groups was sufficiently similar for the equal-variance assumption to be reasonable. A log transformation was considered but did not improve the residual spread, so the untransformed model was retained. The reported power calculation, based on the observed data, exceeded 90%.
crumbs: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment

title: Popcorn Popping Time Experiment
text:
Interpretation and limitations
Because treatment order was randomized and the procedure was controlled, the results support causal conclusions for this specific stovetop setup. They should not be generalized to all popcorn, cooking equipment, or heating conditions. Differences in burner temperature, pan cooldown, and other uncontrolled aspects of the setup may have contributed to variation between trials.
Further work could use temperature-controlled equipment, allow more time between trials, increase the number of replications, and examine additional outcomes such as unpopped kernels, popped volume, or burning.
